segments.say: Oskar is on a late train home, half watching the dark fields slide past the window. Across the aisle, a woman he has never seen before opens her mouth in a huge, slow yawn. He glances at her for a second, then looks away. And then, before he has even decided anything, his own jaw begins to stretch, his eyes squeeze shut, and he is yawning too.

A quick word about Oskar. He's imagined. He's someone we've pictured together, to keep us company tonight. He's thirty-eight, he teaches music at a secondary school, he's just sat through a long parents' evening, and he has an old dog called Pepper who will be waiting behind the front door. Nothing about him stands for any real person, and nothing in his journey is a case study.

Here's what makes it strange. Oskar didn't breathe in that woman's yawn, and she didn't touch him or say a word. All that passed between them was a picture, a few seconds of a stranger's face changing shape. Somehow that picture was enough to set off the same movement in his own body. And if you're feeling a small tug in your jaw right now, you're in very good company.

We'll travel home with Oskar, one stop at a time, and along the way we'll look at what researchers have found. There are diaries kept for a week, ultrasound scans of babies not yet born, people holding packs against their foreheads, strangers stopped on city pavements, and even a group of lions on a game reserve.

show.title: Tonight, we'll explore
items: The oxygen story, put to the test
A slow journey home to sleep

segments.say: Let me say how we'll do this. Every study we mention is a real, published piece of research, and when I give a number, it comes from that research. Where scientists disagree, where a sample was small, or where an idea is still a hypothesis, I'll tell you so. Yawning looks like the simplest thing in the world, and it turns out to be full of open questions.

Let's start by noticing how ordinary this is. You've probably yawned thousands of times in your life. You did it before you could walk or talk. You've done it in classrooms, at kitchen tables and in waiting rooms, sometimes at exactly the wrong moment. And yet, if someone asked you what a yawn is for, you might find that you aren't quite sure.

If that's you, you're in the same position as the scientists. There are several serious ideas about what yawning does, and none of them is settled beyond argument. Some concern waking up and winding down. One concerns the temperature of the brain. Another concerns signalling between members of a group. We'll meet each of them calmly, and weigh what the evidence can and cannot say.

A nearly empty train carriage at night, with warm lamps above the seats and darkness outside the glass. It's a good setting for our question, because it holds everything we need. People are tired, the journey is long and a little dull, and strangers are sitting close enough to see one another's faces. Keep this carriage in mind as we go.

show.cap: A quiet train carriage at night

segments.say: It helps to separate two questions that often get tangled together. The first is why we yawn at all, on our own, when nobody else is doing it. Researchers call that spontaneous yawning. The second is why seeing, hearing or even reading about a yawn can make us yawn. That's called contagious yawning, and it seems to follow some rules of its own.

show.title: Two questions, not one
items: Why do we yawn at all
Why does another person's yawn set ours off

segments.say: The spontaneous kind appears very early in life and is shared widely across the animal world. Dogs do it on the rug. Cats do it after a nap. Many other animals with backbones open their jaws wide in ways that look remarkably familiar. Whatever this movement does, it seems to be old, far older than human language, trains, classrooms or parents' evenings.

The contagious kind is different. It shows up much later in childhood, it varies a great deal from one adult to another, and it has been clearly seen in only a limited number of animal species. That contrast is one of the most interesting clues we have. It suggests that catching a yawn asks something extra of the brain, on top of simply being able to yawn.

You'll often read that somewhere between forty and sixty percent of adults catch a yawn when they watch other people yawning. Treat that as a rough range rather than a law of nature. As we'll see, the figure moves quite a lot depending on how long people watch, how it's measured, who is in the room, and how old the watchers are.

show.title: A commonly quoted range
show.label: of adults are often said to catch yawns from videos

segments.say: Back on the train, Oskar rubs his eyes. He tells himself he isn't going to yawn again, and for a moment he manages it. Then the word itself drifts through his mind, and there it comes, a second yawn, even wider than the first. Across the aisle, the woman has already gone back to her phone. She has no idea what she started.

That's the puzzle we'll carry with us. Something can pass from one person to another without a word, without a touch and often without either of them intending it. It happens between friends, between family members and between strangers on a late train. Understanding even part of how it works tells us something about how closely our bodies pay attention to one another.

show.text: Something that passes between people without a word being said

segments.say: So settle in, wherever you are. If you yawn while you listen, that's completely fine, and honestly rather fitting. There's nothing you need to remember and no test at the end. You can follow every detail, or let the story of the journey carry you along, and drift away whenever it suits you.

show.sub: There's no test at the end

segments.say: Our first stop is the movement itself. Before we ask why a yawn spreads, we should know what it is that's spreading. It lasts only a few seconds, and in that time your jaw, your lungs and your heart all do something unusual. Let's slow it right down and watch it happen.
